en: One to another
They spoke their last farewells:
“If we attack the heaven-favored grim hero,
We are dead.
How shall we ever see alive again
Our poor wives and young children?”
The people lamented amid clamor and grief:
“Whenever it may come, our dear lives
Will end beneath oppression.
Ah, behold this merciless slaughter—
Sit and watch it, father!
We have suffered it through Külchoro.”
All the bearded elders
Of the Jediger lamented without cease,
Amid uproar and grief:
“From our leaders we have always
Suffered grievous humiliation.
Driven forth in disgrace,
Today we shall die by the grim hero’s hand.
From time immemorial until now,
You have attacked the heaven-favored great hero
As though he were an enemy;
Your raising a force against the grim hero—
This deed of yours was wrong.
This Semetey standing here,
The stalwart descended from Manas,
Was a father to us Kyrgyz.
He was our father because
He guarded Ala-Too and made it our homeland;
His father, the gray-maned hero Manas,
Gathered the scattered, wandering Kyrgyz,
Led them and made them a nation;
He waged war against China
And won for the Kyrgyz
Keng-Kol and Talas as their homeland.
How have you Kyrgyz forgotten this?
Can anyone who confronts
The descendant of the native gray-maned Manas,
A grim hero such as this, ever prosper?
Think on this, my wretched people:
Can one who attacks
The lion hero’s son survive?
No man dared cross weapons with
The honored Sultan Semetey.
It was not merely the Kyrgyz people;
I heard that slaughter befell
The Chinese realm, and none escaped.
The warrior-sultan, son of Manas,
Was a lofty, towering mountain pass;
Not only the Kyrgyz, but the whole world
Was guarded by that hero.
Lofty and hard as blood-dark iron—
By God, such a gray-maned hero
No woman will ever bear again.
He would never let the Khagan’s realm destroy us;
He was a dark, gray-maned hero,
A warrior who guarded
Many mighty cities and peoples.
Yet however much we drank from his bounty, we were never sated,
And never abandoned our greed;
Unable ourselves to strike down a wolf,
We could not bear to see a son who did—
Ah, we sly people have not prospered!
From time immemorial until now,
We have never ceased this mischief.
This Sultan Semetey
Was the mountain we relied upon,
The land where our backs found support.
He was a gray stallion that let no horse escape,
And his fortune was perfect.
Your generous-hearted grim hero
Was broader than the face of the earth;
Born in the likeness of a champion,
He would never yield his equal to mortals.
He was a hero who fastened
A stout tassel to his spear.
He guarded the few Arghyn and Kyrgyz,
Letting not even a stirring breeze touch them,
Nor the least chill reach them.
Such was the hero who protected them.
He was a lion and a khan;
When storms came, no wind touched us.
He was the dark, gray-maned hero
Who yielded no livestock to the wrathful.
He was a true brother in valor
To Sultan Manas himself.
To the right were the Russians,
On the frontier were the Chinese,
And ahead stood muskets;
Many were the enemies
Who contended with us.
He guarded us, letting no man with thumbs subdue us,
No creature with claws scratch us,
No winged thing strike us,
And no wrathful foe attack us.
Such was the hero who tended us;
Born in the likeness of a champion,
No equal to him would arise among mortals.
While this grim hero was with us,
Wearing sable hats from the caravan,
We would turn our racehorses’ heads;
By day there was kumiss, by night girls,
And we reveled with thunderous laughter.
We played knucklebones and raised dust,
And when excited, competed at ordo,
Throwing ourselves heartily into the games.
We lived and played at ease;
A whole beaver pelt
We would cut in half
And trim our trouser cuffs with it.
Strutting about as heroes,
Swaggering as though we were gods,
We ate frozen goat fat,
And in our excess devoured barren fillies;
We crunched sugar like snow,
Sipped strong black tea,
And drank distilled liquor.
We camped all along the valley,
With no one to command us,
And lived entirely as we pleased.
We tethered milk-fed camel calves,
And elegantly boiled
Fat lambs and choice heads.
Wearing costly hats of blue lynx,
With swaying ornaments beyond compare,
We spent the days in laughter
And passed the nights in revelry.
While this grim hero was with us,
Did we not live in joy?
His courage and heroism
Grew ever greater as he lived.
Against the teeming Khagan’s realm,
Against the seething Chinese,
He allowed not the slightest calamity
To reach us, but stood guard like a hero.
He was an iron fortress and stronghold;
God will surely never again give
The Kyrgyz another like him.
Why, bristling and pouring out your wrath,
Did you Jediger of the Seven Rivers
Bring calamity upon yourselves?
Among this surging multitude,
Whom of yours had he ever harmed?
Since becoming Semetey,
Since bearing the name Semetey,
Whom among the Jediger of the Seven Rivers
Had he ever injured?
When had he ever invaded your people?
Kyyaz said, ‘March!’
And you wretched, accursed people
Simply obeyed and marched;
You seething Jediger,
Boasting of your strength, took up spears
And rose in tumult.
If the warrior-hero, son of Manas,
Had not carried off your fields,
Had not scattered your treasury,
Had not driven off your wild horses,
Had not strewn your goods from your saddlebags,
Then by obeying Kyyaz’s wicked command,
Attacking the lion hero
And needlessly entangling yourselves in misery,
We have, my people,
Trodden upon
The dragon’s tail.
Can anyone who challenges
This grim hero Semetey prosper?
Can anyone who fights him survive?
Did he not hear of it yesterday—
The late warrior Toltoy?
He was wise and heroic,
A discerning kinsman;
Becoming an outsider among his own kin,
Chynkojo, son of Shygay,
Whose ambition reached across the world,
And Semetey
Were sons of two brothers.
Look at the treachery
Of that swine who died in flames.
Seeking to wage a bitter fight—
Khan Akun was Semetey’s father-in-law,
And Aichürök was his wife—
Chynkojo, son of Shygay,
Truly incited the people
And started a conflict.
Because warrior Toltoy committed that deed,
Many gray-bearded elders
Gathered troops and raised an army,
And all were caught in slaughter.
Terrified before our lord,
We offered our horses in submission
And barely escaped the magnanimous hero.
Chynkojo and Toltoy went mad,
And personally went to attack him;
But all the multitude
Became entangled in unforgiving wrath.
The Jediger, as though eager to die,
Against the grim hero, son of Manas,
Rashly launched the attack themselves.
When had Semetey ever brought hell
Upon your host, Jediger of the Seven Valleys?
When had the grim hero come against us,
Threatening, ‘I will raid your village,’
And brought violence upon us?
By attacking the lion hero,
Today we have entangled ourselves in misery.
It seems we are to die a shameful death.
Whimpering like young pups,
Are we to die miserably?
Raising an uproar all together,
At the hands of that gray-maned prince,
Are we to die dishonorably?
Did we come surging here merely
To scatter and leave this world,
Turning our faces toward Jeti-Suu,
Slaughtered by that peerless lion,
Only to flee away?
We Jediger came surging forth—
Are we not now firm as mountains and stone?
Assailing the panther,
Needlessly entangled in calamity,
Are we to perish in ruin?
With broad reins knotted in a loop,
“Ah, hero, spare our lives!” we shall say—
Are we to cast honor aside, place them
Around our necks, and die?
“Generous lord, spare our lives!”—
Are we to die begging?
Bearded men and elders
Grew anxious and raised an uproar;
All the Jediger and Kipchak wondered,
“How can we ever reach
The bounds of this bloodthirsty man blessed by Kydyr?
Who would dare attack
The lion Manas’s champion
And the people left by that lion?
Who could invade them?” they said.
“He is the son of the great lion;
He will strike me in battle,” they said.
The people clamored, the nation roared;
To recall it, there was great turmoil.
Some men drew close
And spoke among themselves,
While others leaned together
And whispered among themselves.
They returned in grief;
Wretched women and young children asked,
“What will happen now?”
And spoke their last wishes.
When the matter was discussed, great turmoil arose;
The Jediger entered the fray,
Planning with care and reckoning the task;
The Jediger plunged into the uproar.
Some stood stubbornly firm,
Crossing their steel-tipped spears;
Some, in their anguish,
